title: Architecture Data Analysis + Visualization Primer
text:
Designed for complete Python beginners. Load pilot study data, compute simple summaries, and make figures you can reuse in A3/A4 (charts with uncertainty, multi-panel layouts, and a word cloud).

This assumes the repo root contains data/ and scripts/.

from pathlib import Path
import sys
if '__file__' in globals():
    ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
else:
    candidate = Path.cwd()
    if (candidate / 'scripts').exists():
        ROOT = candidate
    elif candidate.name == 'notebooks' and (candidate.parent / 'scripts').exists():
        ROOT = candidate.parent
    else:
        ROOT = candidate
if str(ROOT / 'scripts') not in sys.path:
    sys.path.append(str(ROOT / 'scripts'))

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from scipy import stats

from plotting_utils import set_style, plot_error_bars, wordcloud_from_series
import data_simulation as sim
set_style()




We compare two conditions (A vs. B) for a space.

pilot_path = ROOT / 'data' / 'pilot_observations_fake.csv'
if not pilot_path.exists():
    sim.save_default_fake_data(ROOT)
pilot = pd.read_csv(pilot_path, parse_dates=['timestamp'])
pilot.head()



Summaries and a first line chart.

pilot.describe(include='all')


plt.figure(figsize=(9,4))
sns.lineplot(data=pilot, x='timestamp', y='occupancy_count', hue='condition')
plt.title('Occupancy over time (pilot)')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()





Mean dwell time by condition with 95% CIs.

_ = plot_error_bars(pilot, group_col='condition', value_col='dwell_time_mean_min', title='Dwell time (mean ± 95% CI)')
plt.show()



Independent t-test on dwell time between A and B (pilot scale).

a = pilot.loc[pilot.condition=='A', 'dwell_time_mean_min']
b = pilot.loc[pilot.condition=='B', 'dwell_time_mean_min']
stats.ttest_ind(a, b, equal_var=False)





Box/violin charts communicate variability quickly.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1,2, figsize=(10,4))
sns.boxplot(data=pilot, x='condition', y='occupancy_count', ax=ax[0])
sns.violinplot(data=pilot, x='condition', y='dwell_time_mean_min', ax=ax[1])
ax[0].set_title('Occupancy distribution')
ax[1].set_title('Dwell time distribution')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()




Resample with replacement to estimate uncertainty without heavy math.

def bootstrap_ci(x, n_boot=2000, ci=0.95, seed=42):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    means = []
    for _ in range(n_boot):
        sample = rng.choice(x, size=len(x), replace=True)
        means.append(np.mean(sample))
    lo = np.percentile(means, (1-ci)/2*100)
    hi = np.percentile(means, (1+(ci))/2*100)
    return float(np.mean(means)), float(lo), float(hi)

for cond in ['A','B']:
    m, lo, hi = bootstrap_ci(pilot.loc[pilot.condition==cond, 'dwell_time_mean_min'].values)
    print(cond, 'mean≈', round(m,2), 'CI', (round(lo,2), round(hi,2)))

survey = pd.read_csv(survey_path)

ax.axhline(24, ls='--', c='red', label='Target ≥ 24 users')
ax.set_title('Occupancy (mean ± 95% CI) with target line')
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
out = ROOT / 'docs' / 'fig_occupancy_bar.png'
plt.savefig(out, dpi=200)
out

axs[1,1].set_title('Occupancy mean ± CI')

title: ML Primer: The 12 Principles
text:
What you’ll learn

In plain language A clear mental model of how ML works without math overload — and where it helps (and where it doesn’t) in architectural workflows.


the 12 principles that make ML predictable, not mysterious
how to use generative tools responsibly for studio work
everything reproducible: prompts, seeds, masks, versions


This is the skinned summary. The full detailed deck — pipeline, diffusion, segmentation, surrogate modeling, GH/Honeybee tooling — is the original ML for Architecture PDF.

title: ML Primer: The 12 Principles
text:
How to read each principle
Every principle uses the same four-part frame — the same shape as the course’s own evidence logic:


Idea the principle itself


Why it matters what it changes for you

title: ML Primer: The 12 Principles
section: Principle 1 — ML learns a mapping from examples, not rules
text:
Principle 1 — ML learns a mapping from examples, not rules

Idea An ML model is a function f(x) → y whose parameters are fit from examples (x, y).



Why it matters Expect pattern recognition, not hand-coded logic. The model learns regularities present in the data.


Studio example (massing image) → predicted daylight metric; (facade photo) → style label.



Quick activity · 2 min Name three inputs you could give a model in your current studio project. What output would you want?

title: ML Primer: The 12 Principles
section: Principle 2 — Data is the design brief
text:
Principle 2 — Data is the design brief

Idea The dataset defines what the model can and cannot learn.



Why it matters Better data beats fancier models — curate for coverage and quality, not just quantity.


Studio example A facade-style classifier fails if trained only on one region or era.



Quick activity · 2 min List two gaps in a “facade” dataset that would cause failures on your campus. How would you fill them?

title: ML Primer: The 12 Principles
section: Principle 3 — Representation shapes what can be learned
text:
Principle 3 — Representation shapes what can be learned

Idea How we encode inputs (pixels, meshes, graphs, text) determines what the model can “see”.



Why it matters Choosing a representation is like selecting a drawing type: plan vs section vs perspective.


Studio example Street photos (pixels) for segmentation vs adjacency graphs for layout optimization.



Quick activity · 2 min For your task, would pixels, vectors, meshes, or text be best — and why?

title: ML Primer: The 12 Principles
text:
Principle 4 — Loss = what “better” means

Idea The loss function translates “good” into math; models only improve on what loss rewards.



Why it matters If the loss ignores safety or legibility, the model will too. This is your threshold, made explicit.


Studio example A daylight surrogate with MSE learns averages; worst-case glare needs a different objective.



Quick activity · 2 min Write a one-line “loss” for your project (e.g., minimize peak glare while keeping daylight autonomy above target).

title: ML Primer: The 12 Principles
text:
Principle 5 — Training = reduce loss (gradient descent)

Idea Training iteratively adjusts parameters in the direction that reduces loss.



Why it matters Explains learning rate, convergence, and why training looks rough before it stabilizes.


Studio example Don’t judge early iterations; monitor the validation curve, not the first guesses.



Quick activity · 2 min Sketch how you’d know training is “done” (hint: validation loss / early stopping).

title: ML Primer: The 12 Principles
text:
Principle 6 — Generalization is the goal

Idea We care about performance on new, unseen data — not just the training set.



Why it matters Overfitting = memorization; good models transfer to the next site or city.


Studio example A roof-type detector perfect on your curated set fails on cloudy days.



Quick activity · 2 min Name two differences between training images and deployment images. How will you test generalization?

title: ML Primer: The 12 Principles
section: Principle 7 — Bias–variance: too simple vs too specific
text:
Principle 7 — Bias–variance: too simple vs too specific

Idea Underfit models are too simple; overfit models memorize noise.



Why it matters You control this via model capacity, augmentation, and regularization.


Studio example A tiny model misses brick vs terracotta; a huge model memorizes specific buildings.



Quick activity · 2 min Which knob would you turn first to reduce overfit — augmentation, regularization, or more data?

title: ML Primer: The 12 Principles
section: Principle 8 — Uncertainty is real: treat outputs as suggestions
text:
Principle 8 — Uncertainty is real: treat outputs as suggestions

Idea Predictions are probabilistic; confidence varies by context and input quality.



Why it matters This is the course thesis in ML form: sample multiple outputs and critique; avoid single-image “truth”.


Studio example Use seeds and A/B comparisons for renders, not one lucky frame.



Quick activity · 2 min Generate 3 variations (same seed + small prompt tweaks); choose and justify one.

title: ML Primer: The 12 Principles
text:
Principle 9 — Distribution shift breaks models

Idea When deployment data differ from training (climate, culture, camera), expect failure.



Why it matters Plan pilots on real sites; monitor drift; retrain when needed.


Studio example A Berlin-trained segmenter struggles in Bangkok (materials, colors, sky).



Quick activity · 2 min Write one “shift” you expect in your project and a way to detect it.

title: ML Primer: The 12 Principles
text:
Principle 10 — Generative models = distributions + conditioning

Idea Diffusion models learn a distribution and sample from it; prompts/masks/refs condition the sampling.



Why it matters Prompts steer; seeds give reproducibility; masks and references preserve geometry and identity.


Studio example Keep geometry via masks; change cladding via prompt; reuse the same seed for versions.



Quick activity · 2 min Take a white-model view; list what you’d mask vs what you’d let the model change.

title: ML Primer: The 12 Principles
section: Principle 11 — Evaluation must match the task
text:
Principle 11 — Evaluation must match the task

Idea Pick metrics that reflect the goal and pair them with human A/B judgment for visuals.



Why it matters Numbers alone can reward “pretty wrong” results.


Studio example For concept imagery, use pairwise preference + a rubric (material legibility, camera plausibility).



Quick activity · 2 min Draft two rubric criteria to compare two generated facade images.

title: ML Primer: The 12 Principles
text:
Principle 12 — Ethics, IP, and human-in-the-loop

Idea Datasets carry bias; licenses and privacy matter; designers remain accountable.



Why it matters You choose sources, cite them, disclose process, and keep clients safe.


Studio example Use open/owned references; document prompts, seeds, masks; avoid identifying people without consent.



Quick activity · 2 min Pick one slide of your own and add a visible credit line for every image source.

title: Week 8: Reproducibility and Mentor Prep
section: If you can’t rerun it, it isn’t evidence
text:
If you can’t rerun it, it isn’t evidence
A result becomes evidence only when someone else can inspect how you got it — and ideally reproduce it.

The week’s question If you left the project tomorrow, could someone trust your output without you in the room to explain it?

Documentation is not paperwork after the fact. It is the part of the method that makes the output legible.

title: Week 8: Reproducibility and Mentor Prep
text:
Where reproducibility quietly fails
These are ordinary, not dramatic — and they happen to careful people.







Failure
What was lost




Plugin / version not recorded
the file won’t reopen or rerun later


Settings changed but not noted
results can’t be matched to inputs


One person held the knowledge
nobody else can defend the method


CRS / units left implicit
spatial output is silently wrong


AI-generated step never checked
a claim no one actually understands




The risk is not embarrassment. It is presenting a result you can no longer stand behind.

title: Week 8: Reproducibility and Mentor Prep
text:
A quick, honest poll
Have you ever struggled to reconstruct what you did on a project from a few months ago?

Almost everyone has. The point is not guilt — it is to treat documentation as a normal, expected part of the workflow, starting with one process today.

title: Week 8: Reproducibility and Mentor Prep
section: Document one workflow so it stands alone
text:
Document one workflow so it stands alone
Pick the most complex or critical workflow in your project — the one you would least want to lose.

Do this now · 10 minutes Write step-by-step instructions clear enough that a classmate who has never seen your method could follow them and get your result — with no verbal explanation from you.

Candidates: a Grasshopper setup, a survey-data analysis, a GIS operation, a Python notebook, a statistical step.

title: Week 8: Reproducibility and Mentor Prep
text:
Documentation template
Copy this structure into your notes.



Section
What to fill in




Workflow
the one process you are documenting


Setup
software + versions, files/data, prerequisite skills


Steps
each step, in order, with the reason for it


Decisions
where a choice was made, and why


Troubleshooting
common error → what to do


Quality check
how to know the result is correct

title: Week 8: Reproducibility and Mentor Prep
text:
The documentation swap
We test documentation the only honest way: someone else follows it cold.


Exchange · 2 min Swap with someone whose method differs from yours. No verbal notes — the instructions must stand alone.


Attempt · 8 min Follow their steps exactly. Mark where you get confused, stuck, or have to guess.


Feedback · 5 min Report what was unclear, what was missing, and the one change that would help most.



The gaps you find are the gaps a future reader would hit. This is the most useful feedback you will get all week.

title: Week 8: Reproducibility and Mentor Prep
section: What AI use and research methods share
text:
What AI use and research methods share

The shared root Both come down to one principle: KNOW YOUR DATA.



In research ethics - who your participants are - how the data was collected - the biases in your sample - the limits of your method


In AI use - what the model was trained on - the biases that training carries - what the tool can and cannot do - when its output should not be trusted


When you don’t understand the data behind a result, harm propagates quietly and at scale.

title: Week 8: Reproducibility and Mentor Prep
text:
Automation Ethics Cases
Read each case and place it: acceptable, acceptable with disclosure, or not acceptable — and say why.



Case
The action




1
Using an AI assistant to debug your Python


2
Having AI write your literature-review summary


3
Generating synthetic sample data for testing


4
Automating a calculation you don’t understand




The line is rarely “AI or not.” It is understanding + disclosure: do you understand the step, and have you said how it was produced?

title: Week 8: Reproducibility and Mentor Prep
text:
AI Method Review
A common situation, examined as a method — not a person.

The artifact A building-performance analysis: polished charts, statistics beyond the author’s stated skill, no understanding of the method when questioned, no disclosure of AI use.


Review it together - which specific claims can the author actually defend? - what should have been disclosed, and where? - what verification would have made this trustworthy? - what is the minimum honest version of this output?

We critique the workflow and its claims, never the author’s ability.

title: Week 8: Reproducibility and Mentor Prep
text:
An AI-assisted workflow, made honest
The same four-zone frame as the rest of the course — but now one zone is an AI draft, and the manual check and disclosure are not optional.


Prompt “Write a geopandas script that buffers transit stops 400 m and reports % of site parcels covered.”


AI output a draft script + a Grasshopper Python component stub


Manual check CRS is projected (metres, not degrees); buffer distance correct; parcel counts spot-checked by hand


Disclosure note “Buffer script drafted with AI; CRS and counts verified manually on DD-MM.”



AI can draft the step. It cannot verify it or disclose it. Those two zones are your responsibility, every time.

title: Week 8: Reproducibility and Mentor Prep
text:
Make the mentor meeting count
Most mentor time is lost to vague questions. A little preparation turns a pleasant chat into a useful one.

Prepare now · 15 minutes 1. One-liner — your project in a single sentence 2. Specific ask — the exact advice you need 3. Context check — what your mentor actually does 4. Question bank — five strategic questions 5. Show-and-tell — the one thing you want them to see

title: Week 8: Reproducibility and Mentor Prep
text:
Weak questions vs strategic questions


Weak — wastes the slot - “What do you think of my project?” - “Do you have any advice?” - “How do I get a job in your field?”


Strategic — creates value - “What evidence would convince [specific stakeholder] to change current practice?” - “What implementation barriers am I likely missing?” - “How do practitioners here validate this kind of analysis?” - “What would make my findings most useful to someone in your position?”

title: Week 8: Reproducibility and Mentor Prep
text:
Question workshop

In pairs · 10 minutes 1. Person A delivers their one-liner + best strategic question 2. Person B gives specific feedback and one improvement 3. Swap roles and repeat


You are not competing for the best question. You are pressure-testing your own so it earns a real answer in the room.

Evidence mapping is a decision, not a collection

Evidence categories to sort


Often decisive - published research - standards and code - site observations - open datasets - simulations - maps and spatial layers


Often supporting only - precedent and case studies - interviews or surveys - one-off articles
Useful for framing, rarely enough on their own.


Not every category belongs in every project.

title: Week 6: Evidence and Pathway Mapping
section: Does your route generalize, or only fit this one case?
text:
Does your route generalize, or only fit this one case?

Principle 6 — Generalization is the goal In ML, a model that is perfect on its training set but fails on new data has overfit. A workflow is the same: it must hold up beyond the single case you tuned it on.


So Pick a route whose smallest useful output would still be defensible on a second site, season, or scenario — not just the one that looks good today.

See ML Primer · Principle 6.

GIS is not just digital mapping

location
proximity
overlap
boundaries
access
context over space and time


If the question is not spatial, a beautiful map is decoration, not evidence.

Each one names a spatial claim you would have to defend with evidence.

title: Week 4: GIS Choices for Architects

Minimal geopandas workflow
import geopandas as gpd

sites = gpd.read_file("candidate_sites.geojson")
sites = sites.to_crs(3857)          # state the CRS explicitly
sites["buffer_400m"] = sites.buffer(400)
print(len(sites))                   # spot-check the count
sites.plot(column="score", legend=True)

Decorative map vs decision map


Decorative map Many layers, rich styling, looks professional — but no claim attached. If you removed it, the argument would not change.


Decision map States CRS, names the inputs, reports a number (coverage %, count, distance), and points to one decision it changes.



If the output does not inform a decision, it is just map decoration.

Architecture uses many evidence types
Designers draw on a wide range of inputs. None is automatically strong or weak — strength depends on the decision it served.

precedent

simulation
measurement

title: Week 2: Audit the Evidence You Already Use

Not all inputs are equal

The useful question Did this input actually reduce uncertainty for the decision?

If it did not, it may have been something else wearing the costume of evidence:

inspiration
convention
assumption
noise

title: Week 2: Audit the Evidence You Already Use
text:
A fast evidence ladder
The same input can sit high or low depending on fit. As a rough first sort:


Usually stronger Measured performance · well-matched comparative evidence · relevant standards and verified constraints


Often in between Simulation output · stakeholder input · a single relevant precedent — strong only if assumptions and context hold


Usually weaker Isolated precedent images · vague “best practice” · unsupported confidence from the designer



A weak input is not forbidden — it just cannot carry a strong claim on its own.

title: ARCH7476: Generative Design in Architecture
text:
What Makes This Generative Design
The course treats generative design as a method, not a style.
In this course, generative means:

a documented workflow that creates or varies multiple design options and evaluates them against explicit criteria.

Students learn to define:

what can vary
what must remain fixed
what evidence can evaluate alternatives
what threshold would change a design decision
what workflow can be reused by another person

Supported workflow routes include:







Workflow route
Typical design use




Grasshopper / parametric workflow
create and compare option families


BIM/BEM and simulation literacy
test performance assumptions across scenarios


GIS / spatial workflow
compare site or context alternatives


Python / notebook workflow
evaluate repeated design/data cases


AI-assisted workflow building
accelerate script or workflow components, then verify them


Spreadsheet / low-code workflow
compare variants, sensitivity, and thresholds transparently

title: Course Schedule
text:
Every week has two parts:

a focused lecture or tool demonstration
a studio-lab where students apply that week’s lens to their own project



The second half of class is a Project Reasoning Round Table, not a formal presentation.
Before Session 2, each student uploads one rough material to Slack:

plan, section, render, massing image, or site photo
precedent image or evidence source
table, chart, GIS map, GH canvas, BIM/BEM screenshot, notebook output, or prompt log
draft object card, presentation slide, or reproducibility note

Selected students speak for 60-90 seconds:

I brought ________.
I chose or questioned this evidence/tool because ________.
It supports ________.
It does not yet show ________.
My question to the room is ________.

Volunteers go first and receive participation credit. If more examples are needed, the instructor may use random draw or select materials that make the week’s concept visible. The draw is for a short reasoning check-in, not a polished presentation.

text:
This is not a software course
This course is not organized around software demos.
It is organized around one question:

The course question What evidence would make a design decision more defensible?

Every tool we touch is judged only by how well it answers that.

title: Week 1: Why Evidence Needs a Workflow
section: Look harder at what you already did
text:
Look harder at what you already did
You learn most by examining the reasoning inside work you have already done — not by adding new work. Every week, the same four questions, pointed at that week’s object:


Did What did I actually do, step by step?


Assumed What did I assume at each step?


Risk Where did I not check — where could it break?


Verify What would I verify if I did it again?


The point is not to judge old work. It is to see how its argument was built.

title: Week 1: Why Evidence Needs a Workflow
text:
Evidence needs a workflow

precedent images can be useful, but rarely prove performance on their own
simulation numbers can be precise, but still depend on assumptions
survey comments can be rich, but need context before they generalize
data only becomes useful when the path from input to decision is legible


A finding is evidence only when someone else can inspect how you got it.

title: Week 1: Why Evidence Needs a Workflow
text:
Sometimes evidence is just vibes


A vibe is not useless It is often the first clue that something might matter.


A vibe is not enough by itself It gets stronger only when the next step asks what would confirm, qualify, or challenge it.


For each image next: name the vibe claim, what it does not show yet, and the next evidence move.

Polished restaurant interior, dramatic lighting, visually busy

Smartphone camera preview of a picturesque mountain and lake




The ad-logic problem

title: Week 1: Why Evidence Needs a Workflow

French street at blue hour with trees, lamps, calm road




Perception is partial

Greenery-covered building facade with dense planted wall




The studio render problem

Vibe claim: “This facade is sustainable; the render is green.”


Not shown yet: visual greenness is not environmental performance.


Ask for: solar exposure, heat gain, daylight, irrigation/maintenance, material data.

title: Week 3: Spreadsheet as the Comparison Layer
section: The spreadsheet is the comparison layer
text:
The spreadsheet is the comparison layer
This is not remedial Excel. A workbook is the most portable way to make a generative comparison of variants legible to someone else.

Why it earns its place It is the lowest-friction surface where assumptions, options, and trade-offs sit side by side and stay editable.


visible assumptions, not hidden ones
editable comparison logic anyone can rerun
traceable calculations from input to claim
fast iteration with no heavy setup

title: Week 3: Spreadsheet as the Comparison Layer
section: Where it sits on the spine
text:
Where it sits on the spine

Decision Evidence Variation Output Threshold Action

The workbook is how Variation becomes inspectable: many variants or scenarios, one comparable structure, one readable output.

A1 is finalized this week — the Total Recall board. The comparison habit you build here is exactly what A2’s Workflow Map will formalize.

title: Week 3: Spreadsheet as the Comparison Layer
text:
Workbook anatomy
The same four-zone frame we use for every tool. A real workbook screenshot drops into this later.


Input evidence rows — source, observation, confidence per variant


What varies the option or scenario being compared (A / B / C, or low / mid / high)


Output one chart or matrix that makes the trade-off visible


Quality check units stated, legend present, formulas readable by a stranger



Screenshot pending — we will capture a live workbook in class rather than fake a polished one.

title: Week 3: Spreadsheet as the Comparison Layer
section: Start with the decision, not the software
text:
Start with the decision, not the software
The structure follows the question, never the other way around.


Workbook with no decision - one giant undifferentiated sheet - no units, no audience - columns with no reason to exist


Workbook built on a decision - one question per structure - one row type per sheet - one clear output already in mind

title: Week 3: Spreadsheet as the Comparison Layer
text:
A useful workbook pattern
Three sheets, each tied to one job in the comparison.


Sheet 1 · Evidence log source · date · evidence type · relevance · confidence


Sheet 2 · Alternatives option · criteria · scores or ranges · comments


Sheet 3 · Outputs the chart · the matrix · the summary line



Each sheet answers one question, so the reader never has to reverse-engineer your intent.

title: Week 3: Spreadsheet as the Comparison Layer
text:
From image to comparable fields



High Line, New York


If you claimed this public-space strategy works, what would the workbook need to compare? Move from atmosphere to comparable fields: location, activity type, time and duration, seating/circulation, weather, evidence source and confidence.

title: Week 3: Spreadsheet as the Comparison Layer
text:
Typical comparison uses

precedent comparison across variants
evidence and source logging
option scoring with stated criteria
uncertainty-range charts
summary tables for a decision brief


Every one of these is a way of laying variants side by side so the trade-off becomes visible to someone who was not in your head.

title: Week 3: Spreadsheet as the Comparison Layer
text:
Bad chart vs cleaned chart
A chart fails when it describes data instead of carrying a message.


The chart that fails a stakeholder - too many series, no dominant takeaway - labels too small to read at a glance - colour decorating instead of working - title naming the data, not the message


The cleaned chart - one message, stated in the title - only the series that support it - annotation forcing the eye to the point - uncertainty shown where it matters

title: Week 3: Spreadsheet as the Comparison Layer
text:
The 3-second message test
If a critic glances for three seconds, can they tell:

what is being compared?
which option is stronger or riskier?
what they are meant to notice?


If not, the chart is not finished — that is a clarity gap, not a failure of taste.

title: Week 3: Spreadsheet as the Comparison Layer
text:
Chart rescue formula


Message Decide the one thing the chart must say


Remove Cut everything that does not support it


Force Use annotation or labels to make the point unmissable


Limit Show uncertainty, then connect back to the decision

title: Week 3: Spreadsheet as the Comparison Layer
text:
Show uncertainty honestly


Avoid - fake precision - unexplained weighted scores - single-point claims on weak inputs


Prefer - ranges and scenario labels - note fields for assumptions - charts that make limits visible

title: Week 3: Spreadsheet as the Comparison Layer
section: When you weight a decision matrix, you are writing a loss function
text:
When you weight a decision matrix, you are writing a loss function

Principle 4 — Loss = what “better” means An ML model only improves on what its loss rewards. Your spreadsheet’s weights are the same thing: they define what “better” means before you compare anything.


So If your weighting ignores a real constraint (cost, daylight, legibility), the “winning” variant will too. Make the criterion explicit, like a loss.

See ML Primer · Principles 3–4.

where BIM/BEM workflows break in practice


A simulation number is only as good as the assumptions and cleanup behind it.

title: Week 5: BIM, BEM, and Building Performance
text:
What are BIM and BEM?


BIM

digital model of physical and functional building characteristics
serves design, construction, coordination, and facility management
prioritizes geometry, materials, relationships, and documentation



BEM

computational model of thermal behavior and energy flows
serves analysis, optimization, and compliance
prioritizes zones, schedules, systems, weather, and performance assumptions

title: Week 5: BIM, BEM, and Building Performance
text:
Same building, different core questions


BIM asks What do we build, where does it go, and how is it put together?


BEM asks How will it behave over time when weather, people, and systems act on it?

title: Week 5: BIM, BEM, and Building Performance
text:
Same building, two models


BIM view walls · rooms · floors · doors · material layers · element relationships


BEM view thermal zones · heat-transfer surfaces · schedules · weather · HVAC systems


Shared object the same wall exists in both — but not for the same reason


Quality check does each model carry what its analysis actually needs?



Commonly fails to translate Thermal zoning, occupancy and system schedules, real constructions (R-value, SHGC, mass), and building orientation.

text:
The prototype frame — four zones
Read any workflow as four zones. If you can fill all four honestly, you have a prototype, not just a file.


Input the real files, data, or model the method starts from


What varies the one thing you change between runs


Output the single interpretable result it produces


Quality check what proves the run was valid, not just that it ran



A screenshot of your tool running drops into this frame once you have one. Until then it stays marked pending — honest, not faked.

title: Week 7: Method Prototype Studio
text:
Reproducibility lessons from practice
The common failures are not about talent — they are about traceability.

the analyst leaves and no one can rerun the method
the spreadsheet works on one machine only
the GIS layers were clipped somehow but nobody recorded how
the notebook runs, but only if you know which file was silently edited


If the workflow cannot be retraced, the result is hard to trust — no matter how good the output looks.

title: Week 7: Method Prototype Studio
text:
Where the gaps usually hide
Typical first-draft descriptions sound like this:

“I used some plugin, but I forgot which one.”
“I changed the settings until it looked right.”
“The chart came from another file, I think.”
“The model worked last week.”


Each of these is a missing line in one of the four zones. Naming the gap is the first repair.

title: Week 7: Method Prototype Studio
section: There is no single correct technical route
text:
There is no single correct technical route
Six routes, same four zones. None is more “advanced” than the others — each is judged only by whether the loop is legible.


Spreadsheet In comparison table · Varies parameter ranges · Out ranked options · Check formulas auditable, units stated


GIS In layers + CRS · Varies operation sequence · Out spatial comparison · Check CRS stated, counts spot-checked


Python / notebook In data files + paths · Varies analysis parameters · Out figure / table · Check runs top-to-bottom, paths stated




GH / parametric In geometry + sliders · Varies the design space · Out comparable variants · Check variants share assumptions


BIM/BEM / simulation In model + settings · Varies scenario assumptions · Out performance result · Check dominant assumptions documented


AI-assisted In prompt + source data · Varies what AI generates / edits · Out drafted component · Check a manual review confirms it



Pick the route that makes your decision more defensible — not the one that looks most impressive.

When good research goes bad
Strong work can still fail at the moment it reaches an audience.


Case 1 · method over message - great method - weak message - the audience hears process, not action


Case 2 · correct but unclear - technically correct charts - no clear takeaway - the status quo survives because the room stays confused

The test Could you explain your semester in two slides to a busy critic, client, or studio tutor who gives you three minutes?

If not, your findings are still trapped inside your process.

section: One useful story structure for busy stakeholders
text:
One useful story structure for busy stakeholders


What problem or decision matters?
What evidence did you gather?
What changed because of that evidence?
What should happen next?


This is not simplification for its own sake. It is decision support.

title: Week 9: Storytelling, Figures, and Decisions

Start with their problem

Begin with - the decision - the stake - the missing evidence

Give your figure three seconds. Can a viewer tell:


what is being compared?
which side performs better?
what the implication is?


If not, it needs revision.

title: Week 9: Storytelling, Figures, and Decisions
text:
Figure rescue: before and after


Before · the weak figure - five series, no focus - title reads “Results — Final” - legend the reader must decode - error bars buried or absent - nothing ties it to a decision


After · the cleaned figure - one message, two series compared - title states the takeaway in words - the winning option labelled directly - uncertainty shown where it matters - a caption naming the design action

connect the figure to the design decision

title: Week 9: Storytelling, Figures, and Decisions
text:
Object-card anatomy
The whole card is built around one dominant recommendation. Everything else supports it.


1 · The dominant recommendation The one sentence the viewer must leave with. Largest, first, unmissable.


2 · One comparison figure A single legible chart that shows the comparison behind the recommendation — secondary to the headline, never competing with it.




3 · One threshold sentence The rule that turns the comparison into a decision: “we prefer X once the gain clears Y.”


4 · One limitations note Where the evidence is weakest and what would change the conclusion — small, honest, present.

text:
Treat a model output as a suggestion, and match the metric to the task


Principle 8 — Uncertainty is real Predictions are probabilistic. Sample multiple outputs and critique; avoid presenting one lucky frame as truth.


Principle 11 — Evaluation must match the task Numbers alone can reward “pretty wrong” results. Pair a metric with human A/B judgment for visuals.



So State your threshold WITH its uncertainty, and make the figure show the comparison — not a single hero result.

See ML Primer · Principles 8 & 11.

title: Week 11: Final Package Clinic
text:
Four components, one package
A4 is not one document. It is four linked components, each answering a different question. Polish here means each one answers its question clearly.


1 · Practice Case The applied story: a real decision and what changed because of the evidence.
Answers: what changed?


2 · Research Brief The reasoning and evidence behind the recommendation, stated honestly.
Answers: how do you know?




3 · Object Card The single readable artifact a viewer meets at the fair.
Answers: what does a viewer see?


4 · Reproducibility Capsule The inputs, steps, and files so the method can be inspected.
Answers: how can someone inspect the method?

title: Week 11: Final Package Clinic
text:
How the components fit together
The four components are not parallel deliverables — they answer four questions a reviewer asks in sequence.





flowchart LR
    PC[Practice Case<br/>what changed?] --> RB[Research Brief<br/>how do you know?]
    RB --> OC[Object Card<br/>what does a viewer see?]
    OC --> RC[Reproducibility Capsule<br/>how can someone inspect the method?]
    RC --> A4[A4: Workflow Package]







If a stranger can walk this chain without you in the room, the package is done. Networking is secondary — the package comes first.

Polish is not decoration. It is making each link legible.

title: Week 11: Final Package Clinic
text:
Object Card refinement
The Object Card is the one artifact most viewers actually read. It must stand alone.


What it must carry - the decision and who it is for - one figure that carries the message - the recommendation, in plain language - a stated limit


The 30-second test Hand your draft card to a neighbour. Can they state your recommendation and one limit after 30 seconds, without you speaking?

title: Week 11: Final Package Clinic
text:
Sharpen the writing
The Research Brief and Practice Case carry the argument. Tighten them.

8-minute writing pass 1. Opening — does the first paragraph state the decision, finding, and action? 2. Thread — is the stakeholder’s relevance clear all the way through? 3. Evidence — is confidence matched to the strength of the evidence? 4. Citations — are sources complete and the capsule index linked?


State uncertainty plainly. Overclaiming weakens credibility faster than admitting a limit ever will.

title: Week 11: Final Package Clinic
text:
The message-clarity clinic
Pair up. One reads as a busy reader; the other presents the core message.

Role-play, 4 minutes The reader skims, then asks: “So what should I actually do?” The presenter must answer in one sentence.


The one-thing test If a reader remembers only one thing, what should it be? Does every part of your package support that one message?

title: Week 11: Final Package Clinic
text:
Prepare for the likely questions
Most fair questions fall into three families. Draft one honest answer for each.


Method “How do you know the sample / model is adequate?” → state your check and its limit.


Implementation “What would this cost or take to apply?” → give a range, not a guess.


Alternatives “Could something else explain this?” → name the alternative you ruled out, and how.



A question is a chance to show your reasoning, not an attack to defend against. Acknowledging a limit builds more credibility than deflecting.

title: Week 11: Final Package Clinic
section: A useful answer, in four moves
text:
A useful answer, in four moves

The response shape 1. Acknowledge — “Good question about .” 2. Answer — ”Here is what I found / checked.” 3. Connect — ”What this means for your decision is .” 4. Offer — “I can follow up with the detail in the capsule.”

Keep it short. A clear, honest answer beats a long defensive one.

title: Python + ML Basics for Architects
text:
A fast, friendly introduction to Python, data handling, and simple machine learning — using fake but architecture-flavored data.
Goals: - Learn Python + pandas basics - Load and explore a dataset about windows/daylight/energy - Split into train/test, fit simple models, and evaluate - Understand cross-validation and overfitting with visuals - Get a small taste of neural nets via an MLP (“deep learning vibe”)


If you are on a fresh environment, you may need to install packages (run one by one if needed):
# !pip install pandas numpy matplotlib seaborn scikit-learn scipy wordcloud
This notebook expects the repository structure with a data/ and scripts/ folder.

from pathlib import Path
import sys, warnings

# Add repo root and scripts to import path when running from notebooks/
if '__file__' in globals():
    ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
else:
    candidate = Path.cwd()
    if (candidate / 'scripts').exists():
        ROOT = candidate
    elif candidate.name == 'notebooks' and (candidate.parent / 'scripts').exists():
        ROOT = candidate.parent
    else:
        ROOT = candidate
if str(ROOT / 'scripts') not in sys.path:
    sys.path.append(str(ROOT / 'scripts'))

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, KFold, cross_val_score
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, PolynomialFeatures
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, Ridge
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score, mean_absolute_error
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, confusion_matrix
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPClassifier

from plotting_utils import set_style, plot_cv_folds, confusion_matrix_plot, learning_curve_plot, validation_curve_plot
import data_simulation as sim

set_style()
np.random.seed(42)




Python stores numbers, strings, lists, and dictionaries. You’ll mostly use lists/dicts and then pandas DataFrames.

# Lists and dicts
sizes = [10, 20, 30]
room = {"name": "Studio A", "area_m2": 120, "seats": 40}
sizes.append(40)
{"sizes": sizes, "room": room}


# Numpy and pandas basics
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
a = np.array([1,2,3])
df = pd.DataFrame({"x": [1,2,3], "y": [3,2,1]})
df.describe()




We use fake data that mimics window-to-wall ratio (wwr), shading depth, orientation, and energy/daylight outcomes.

data_path = ROOT / 'data' / 'building_performance_fake.csv'
if not data_path.exists():
    # Generate defaults if missing
    sim.save_default_fake_data(ROOT)

df = pd.read_csv(data_path)
df.head()


df.describe(include='all')


sns.pairplot(df[['wwr','shading_depth_m','daylit_area','glare_probability','cooling_kwh_m2']])
plt.suptitle('Quick relationships', y=1.02);




We fit a simple linear model and evaluate on a held-out test set.

features = ['wwr','shading_depth_m','orientation','glazing_u_w_m2k']
target = 'cooling_kwh_m2'
X = df[features]
y = df[target]

cat = ['orientation']
num = ['wwr','shading_depth_m','glazing_u_w_m2k']
pre = ColumnTransformer([
    ("cat", OneHotEncoder(drop='first'), cat),
    ("num", 'passthrough', num)
])

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=42)
reg = Pipeline([('pre', pre), ('model', LinearRegression())])
reg.fit(X_train, y_train)
pred = reg.predict(X_test)
r2 = r2_score(y_test, pred)
mae = mean_absolute_error(y_test, pred)
r2, mae


plt.scatter(y_test, pred, alpha=0.8)
plt.xlabel('Actual cooling kWh/m²')
plt.ylabel('Predicted')
plt.title(f'Linear Regression: R²={r2:.2f}, MAE={mae:.1f}')
m = np.array([y_test.min(), y_test.max()])
plt.plot(m, m, 'k--', alpha=0.5)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()




Define a simple label: comfortable if glare_probability < 0.35 and daylit_area > 0.5.

df['comfortable'] = ((df['glare_probability'] < 0.35) & (df['daylit_area'] > 0.5)).astype(int)
Xc = df[['wwr','shading_depth_m','orientation']]
yc = df['comfortable']
pre_c = ColumnTransformer([
    ("cat", OneHotEncoder(drop='first'), ['orientation']),
    ("num", 'passthrough', ['wwr','shading_depth_m'])
])
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(Xc, yc, test_size=0.25, random_state=42, stratify=yc)
clf = Pipeline([('pre', pre_c), ('model', LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))])
clf.fit(Xtr, ytr)
predc = clf.predict(Xte)
acc = accuracy_score(yte, predc)
cm = confusion_matrix(yte, predc)
acc, cm


confusion_matrix_plot(cm, class_names=("Not Comfortable","Comfortable"), title=f'Logistic Regression (Accuracy={acc:.2f})');




We vary model complexity (polynomial degree) and show CV scores.

deg_scores = []
cv = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
for deg in range(1,7):
    poly = PolynomialFeatures(degree=deg, include_bias=False)
    pipe = Pipeline([('pre', pre), ('poly', poly), ('ridge', Ridge(alpha=1.0))])
    scores = cross_val_score(pipe, X, y, cv=cv, scoring='r2')
    deg_scores.append((deg, scores.mean(), scores.std()))

ds = pd.DataFrame(deg_scores, columns=['degree','cv_mean','cv_std'])
plt.errorbar(ds['degree'], ds['cv_mean'], yerr=ds['cv_std'], fmt='o-')
plt.xlabel('Polynomial degree (complexity)')
plt.ylabel('CV R²')
plt.title('Overfitting demo: watch CV score peak then drop')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
ds



Each row is a fold; green cells are train, red cells are test.

cv2 = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=7)
_ = plot_cv_folds(n_samples=len(X), cv_splits=cv2.split(np.arange(len(X))), title='5-fold CV: train vs test membership')
plt.show()





A small neural network classifier. This is just to build intuition — it’s not magic, and simple models are often enough.

mlp = Pipeline([('pre', pre_c), ('mlp', MLPClassifier(hidden_layer_sizes=(16,8), max_iter=1000, random_state=42))])
mlp.fit(Xtr, ytr)
acc_mlp = accuracy_score(yte, mlp.predict(Xte))
acc, acc_mlp



How performance improves with more data.

_ = learning_curve_plot(clf, Xc, yc, cv=5, scoring='accuracy')
plt.show()






Always hold out test data or use cross-validation
Start simple; only add complexity if it improves validated performance
Document random seeds and settings for reproducibility
“Deep” models need more data and care; don’t overfit
